text: Hello, everybody. My name is Dima Mazarin,
and I want to talk today how to use
local scientific name resolution and reconciliation
with Gen vérifier.
So what is Gen vérifier?
It is a scientific name reconciliation program.
It uses advanced algorithms that allow to do
partial and fuzzy matching,
also authorship matching.
It has a massive scale. We have pre-indexed more than
80 million records across more than 100 popular
biodiversity datasets.
It has a high throughput.
We have
a system that allows to run more than
2,000 names per second.
And now it has a local or remote support,
which means Gen vérifier can either run locally
or you can use centralized service at
vérifierglobalnames.org.
So why would somebody want to use Gen vérifier locally
if it is available as a service on the web?
The first reason,
there might be no particular dataset that you
need.
It can be that a dataset is proprietary, it can
be institutional,
or it can be specialized dataset that only you use.
When Gen vérifier runs locally, you do not need
network, you don't need internet,
and that can be useful if you are traveling or
if you are in the field.
It is also possible to update particular
dataset of interest
as many times as you want.
And for example,
you want to
update a particular dataset, but in
a centralized service, it will only be updated in a few
months.
Also,
for local Gen vérifier, you don't need the same
datasets as a centralized service.
You can only put datasets that you need
for your particular purposes,
and that will make application run faster.
The main thing about Gen vérifier
is to import data.
It has to be done regularly.
The way we did it before,
we used
datasets from everywhere,
and we had diverse or non-standard formats.
The parsing of these datasets could be complex,
and digestion can be not easy.
If there are minor errors, we might spend
half a day to fix a particular error.
For example,
there can be encoding problems
or metadata
is not
written correctly in XML file in Darwin Core
It can be that
field delimiter has problems in a file,
or it can be that a CSV file, comma-separated file,
does not have consistent number of fields,
and we have to figure out
how to do ingestion correctly.
The way we do it now, we use an application called GNDB.
This application
is part of SF WORK
program that we developed at Species File Group.
GNDB uses unified standard, which means
it can be highly automated how we ingest files.
It has a much higher performance than previous system.
For example, we are able to ingest catalog of life in a matter
of minutes instead of hours, as it was before.
We have a consistent workflow.
So if we have a system
on a
centralized or if you
use it locally,
the workflow is exactly the same. There is no any difference.
We have flexible sources.
We can ingest file from local hard drive, or
we can ingest file from the web.
The system allows to convert with
ease Darwin Core files, ColDP files,
tab and comma-separated files, and so on.
So
let us explain
what GNDB is and what SF WORK
project is.
SF WORK is an active approach to a data
standard.
At the core of SF WORK, there is a
SFGA format.
And the difference between SFGA format and other
biodiversity formats
or standards
is that
we can use SFGA as soon as we downloaded
it.
It doesn't require additional step of converting it
into a database.
And there are all kind of functionality, all kind of
applications that can use this file directly.
In our case, with GNDB,
we do aggregation. So GNDB is an
aggregator of several SFGA files
into one database.
How does it work?
At first, we have several
databases, several datasets in a
variety of formats. It can be just a
text, or it can be tab-separated file,
comma-separated file, ColDP, or Darwin Core
file.
We have program called SF, and we have program Harvester.
We use both of them to
convert all this variety of formats into
SFGA format.
And when we have all the SFGA files that we need,
we run GNDB
to use these files and populate
GN Verifier database, which is currently Postgres.
As soon as database is ready, we can run GN Verifier
directly.
And when we do that, we will have a web interface
to name reconciliation,
command line interface, and also API.
So you can write scripts that will use this local
service.
So what do we do
to add metadata to
these
newly ingested
datasets, which are not in the
official GN Verifier?
To make sense of these datasets,
you would need to enter metadata information
in a YAML file.
As soon as this metadata is created,
GNDB will be able to understand it and
add it to the GN Verifier database.
All the datasets that are
not official should be with ID
1,000 or larger
to avoid conflict.
So here are example commands.
First command, SF command,
takes a Darwin Core file and converts it into
SFGA file,
zipped version. We zip it for
just making it smaller.
The next command, GNDB populate, uses ID
of that new dataset
and sends
its data into
GN Verifier database.
After all the datasets are
imported into
database, we have to run GNDB optimize.
It creates several additional tables, and it
also creates a view which denormalizes the
data.
Denormalization is important for speed
After that, we run
GN Verifier service. It is called Gnames.
And when GN Verifier API service is running,
we can start GN Verifier as a web service
using command gn-verify -p
with the name of the port where it will run, or we can use
GN Verifier directly as a command line system.
Both work the same.
We are
ready to support this new functionality.
It is new,
and we understand it
can be
hard to start using it. So we are happy
to help people to set up GNDB locally.
We are
happy to help.
And as I said before, the system on a local
machine and the system to run Verifier
globalnames.org are exactly the same.
We are still doing active development, and your feedback will
help us to support more dataset formats,
and it will help us to understand how to
streamline the pipeline better.
